reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A bilateral anterior segment dysgenesis characterised by iris and drainage-angle anomalies with a high risk of glaucoma
Ocular signs include a prominent, anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line (posterior embryotoxon), iris strands bridging the angle, iris hypoplasia, corectopia and polycoria
Roughly half of affected individuals develop glaucoma, often in childhood or early adulthood, so lifelong pressure monitoring is essential
Usually autosomal dominant, most commonly from mutations in the transcription factors PITX2 and FOXC1
Systemic features (the Rieger phenotype) include dental anomalies such as small or missing teeth, and redundant periumbilical skin and midface changes
PITX2 mutations are particularly associated with the dental and umbilical systemic features
The condition is one end of the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum that overlaps with Peters anomaly
reference.pathophysiology: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome results from abnormal development of neural-crest-derived tissues forming the anterior segment of the eye, driven by mutations in developmental transcription-factor genes such as PITX2 and FOXC1. Faulty migration and differentiation of these cells produces incomplete regression and anomalous development of structures at the iridocorneal angle and iris, giving the characteristic angle strands, prominent Schwalbe line and iris defects. Maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork and drainage angle impairs aqueous outflow, leading to raised intraocular pressure and glaucoma. The same transcription factors act in the development of teeth, the umbilicus and midface, explaining the associated systemic features.
additionalDifferentials: Peters anomaly within the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum
Aniridia with angle and iris abnormalities
Posterior embryotoxon as an isolated benign finding
Congenital iris hypoplasia from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy to define iris and angle anomalies
Intraocular pressure measurement with regular monitoring for glaucoma
Optic disc assessment and visual field testing where glaucoma is suspected
Dental and systemic examination for the Rieger phenotype
Molecular genetic testing of PITX2 and FOXC1 with family assessment
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or optic disc cupping indicating glaucoma
Progressive visual field loss from uncontrolled glaucoma
Corneal enlargement or clouding in an infant suggesting early glaucoma
Family history of anterior segment anomalies and glaucoma indicating dominant inheritance
reference.prognosis: The ocular anomalies themselves are static, but glaucoma is common, may be difficult to control, and is the principal threat to vision; with early detection and effective pressure control the visual prognosis is good, whereas late or refractory glaucoma can cause irreversible optic nerve damage.
pitfalls: Regarding posterior embryotoxon or iris changes as benign and not screening for glaucoma
Assuming the glaucoma is a one-off, when lifelong surveillance is required
Overlooking the systemic dental and umbilical features that support the diagnosis
Failing to examine and counsel relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
